title: Shared activity between 8 mouse visual areas used fewer dimensions than within one area in all 58 mice; axon projection density did not predict its strength in the pre-set discovery test
abstract: Question: does activity of one mouse visual area predict a second area through a low-dimensional 'communication subspace', as in macaque V1-V2, and does the tracer axon projection density between the areas (Knox et al. 2019) set the strength or dimension of this communication? Data: Allen Visual Coding Neuropixels, 32 Brain Observatory mice (discovery) and 26 Functional Connectivity mice (replication), 20,620 good units in VISp, VISl, VISrl, VISal, VISpm, VISam, LGd and LP; spontaneous activity and trial residuals during drifting gratings. Method: for each session and directed area pair, 25 source and 15 target units, ridge and reduced-rank regression with 10-fold block cross-validation (100 ms bins); pre-set models with session, source-area, target-area, distance and rate terms; mouse bootstrap and area-label permutation. Results: between-area prediction used 2.2-2.9 dimensions against 3.9-4.8 within one area, lower in 115 of 116 mouse-condition sets, and still 1.3-1.7 lower at matched R2. The predictive dimensions aligned less with the source's dominant dimensions than within-area prediction did (exploratory). The pre-set density test failed in the discovery cohort (slope 0.10 log R2 per log10 density, 95% CI -0.07 to 0.28, permutation p = 0.24) but was positive in the replication cohort (0.40, CI 0.05 to 0.94, p = 0.017). The pooled slope was 0.21 (bootstrap CI above 0, permutation p = 0.07). Density did not predict the number of dimensions or the asymmetry, and its slope did not change between spontaneous activity and gratings. Limitations: no receptive-field overlap control, only 8 areas with a narrow density range, tracer data from other mice, zero-lag models.
